analysis:
The reviewed units are test-fixture data in fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json, lines 53488-55090. They hold token ID arrays, repeated-token "cache" prompts, plan block-boundary chain hashes, and a prompt_contract_id for the qwen3.6-35b-a3b-vl-mtp-mxfp8 long_prompt vector (long_prompt at 54092, plan at 54125-54147). The visible file_changes excerpt shows another vector gaining "additional_context": {"enable_thinking": false}, and prompt_token_count, chain hashes and token_ids changing for it (e.g. 803 to 767 tokens, with one fewer cache block boundary). Together with the many small changes at other ranges, this suggests the prompt-rendering contract was regenerated, probably so that the template input carries enable_thinking=false.

The fixtures contain no secrets, keys, credentials or real user data. Their prompts are synthetic strings and the dates are fixed. No code, authorization, attestation, encryption or trust-boundary logic is touched, so TB-002, TB-011 and the A-0xx assets are unaffected.

The one security-relevant link is T-041 (prefix-cache sharing and timing oracle). The chain hashes and prompt_contract_id bind cache identity to the rendered prompt. If the fixtures were regenerated consistently with the code, cache keys stay bound to the new rendering, so there is no regression visible in these units.

Remaining integration question: confirm that the Swift and Go consumers of these vectors compute identical chain hashes and token IDs. That includes the enable_thinking template behavior and the 1025-token vector, so that a cache-key mismatch does not cause a silent mix-up or reuse. This cannot be checked from the fixture alone, and the supplied patch excerpt is truncated.
